At the top, include the customer's name, best phone number, and email address, with a note that email is optional. Add the date the order is placed, the requested pickup date, and a pickup time. We are open Tuesday through Sunday, from 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. for pickups. A customer should be able to enter a preferred time, but the form should not make it sound like that time is already confirmed. Leave a staff-only space to write the confirmed pickup time after checking the calendar. There should also be a place for the staff member who took the order to put their initials.

For the order itself, provide space for the product name, quantity, size or serving count, and price. Cake orders need a line for flavor, filling, frosting, and a short description of decoration. We offer 6-inch, 8-inch, and 10-inch round cakes, as well as quarter-sheet and half-sheet cakes. The form can list those choices, but it should leave room for a different size to be requested. If a customer asks for writing on a cake, provide a box for the exact wording, and label it so staff know to copy the customer's wording rather than correct it. If no writing is requested, leave that box blank rather than filling it with a dash.

The form also needs to distinguish between requests we can plan for and things that are confirmed. A customer can request a color or a particular style, but that doesn't mean we have promised it. Please include a notes field for those requests and a separate staff field for whether the bakery can accommodate them. One customer recently said, "simple flowers, nothing too tall," and another asked for a blue cake but said, "any shade is fine." Ask the customer to list any allergy or dietary concern, and include a checkbox for "No allergy or dietary concerns reported." If a concern is listed, staff should not treat the checkbox as checked. The form should direct staff to review the concern with the baker before confirming the order. We use shared equipment, so the form must not imply that we can guarantee an allergen-free product. For a phone order, staff should write the customer's words as closely as possible and read them back before ending the call.

2. Include a payment section that records the quoted total, deposit received, remaining balance, and payment method. We accept cash and card in the shop, and customers may pay the full amount when ordering or pay a deposit. A deposit is $10 for orders under $50 and 25 percent of the quoted total for orders of $50 or more. If the order total changes after the customer approves a change, staff should update the quoted total and remaining balance; otherwise, they should leave those amounts as originally recorded. Some orders change after they are placed, especially decoration details or the number of items in a pastry tray. Include a change log with the date, the requested change, the staff member who discussed it, and whether the customer approved any change in price. Do not make the form suggest that a requested change is accepted just because it has been written down. If a change affects the price, staff should tell the customer the revised amount and record whether the customer approved it. If the customer does not approve the revised price, keep the original order details and mark the change as not approved, rather than replacing the original details.

This matters because the printed pickup date alone could otherwise look like a promise. Include a space to record the baker's response and the time staff checked.

On paper, there should be enough writing room for an order with more than one product, and staff should be able to attach a second page without losing the customer's name or pickup date. For the digital version, use checkboxes only where more than one choice is genuinely available, and keep the fields for written descriptions open for typing. We are making a catalogue for the photographs kept by the Morrow family, and this recording is for the section on the cedar chest in the upstairs hall. The chest belonged to my grandmother Evelyn, and it held prints from both sides of the family, not just her own albums. The small brass key is still in the blue dish on the hall table, and the chest is not to be moved until we finish checking the labels because the bottom drawer sticks if it is tilted.

The first envelope is marked “River Picnic,” and the date looks like July 1968, although the writing is faint. On the back of one print, Uncle Peter is standing beside the striped tent, and my mother is holding a tin cup. The child near the water is probably Joan, but we should leave the name uncertain until Aunt Ruth checks it. The picture was taken at Miller Bend, not Miller Beach, as I first said. Miller Bend was the family name for the turn in the river below the old footbridge, and there was no beach there.

The people in the picnic picture are Peter Morrow, Ruth Ellis, Evelyn Morrow, and three children. The boy in the checked shirt might be Dan, but the face is partly hidden by the paper napkin. There are two copies of the same frame. One is darker and has a crease across the lower corner. Do not discard the darker one because the crease is visible in the original album, too, and may help us match the print later. The envelope also contains a small grocery receipt dated July 14, but it is not proof that the picnic happened on that day.

I asked Nina about the woman in the green coat, and she said, “That’s my mother before she got her hair cut shorter.” I said, “Right,” meaning that answers the question about the coat, not the date. Nina recognizes the coat from a picture of Evelyn at the railway station. She does not remember the station name, and nobody should add one to the catalogue yet. There is a handwritten note reading, “Bring the wool blanket back to Ruth,” which might connect the picnic to the blanket in the next envelope, but we do not know that for certain.

The next group is winter visits from about 1976 through 1981, and the photographs are mixed together rather than sorted by year. One picture shows a cake with candles and the number nine, but we cannot tell whose birthday it was. In the margin, someone wrote, “December at home.” The dining room curtains are different from the ones in the later photographs, so this may be before the house was painted cream. Please note that the color comparison is a clue and not a confirmed date.

Numbered section for the catalogue decisions:
1. Record the envelope label exactly as “River Picnic,” and keep Miller Bend as the location with a question mark until Ruth confirms the child.
2. Describe the duplicate print as darker with a crease at the lower corner, and retain both copies.
3. Leave the green coat photograph attached to Evelyn only as Nina’s identification, and do not supply a railway station name.
4. Keep the birthday picture in the winter visits group without assigning it to a person or a year.

We found three negatives in a paper sleeve marked “Peter camera.” The word “camera” may be a reminder rather than a maker’s name, so put it in the notes and not in the photographer field. Peter used a box camera that he bought secondhand and said it sometimes left a pale stripe along the edge. The negatives have that stripe, but the print from the birthday scene does not have enough detail to tell whether it came from one of them. The sleeve was inside the same drawer as the winter photographs, although that does not establish that every negative belongs to that group.

At the bottom of the chest was a postcard from Lisbon with no year on it. My cousin Miguel read the writing aloud and said, “A gente vai guardar essa caixa na sala.” He explained that in his family’s casual Portuguese this means, “We are going to keep this box in the room.” The card may refer to the cedar chest, but the word caixa could mean another box, so list the phrase and Miguel’s explanation without claiming it identifies the chest. The postmark says Lisbon, and the message is addressed to Evelyn at her old street address.

There is also a note in German in Peter’s handwriting: “Er kommt um sechs.” Ruth says that means, “He comes at six,” and that Peter often wrote down a train arrival time for somebody collecting a visitor. We do not know who he is or which day the note refers to, so do not connect it to the railway station photograph. The note was folded around a small ticket stub, and the printed date on the stub is too worn to read.

One important condition: if Aunt Ruth confirms that the child by the river is Joan, then add Joan’s name to that photograph’s caption, but leave the location as Miller Bend and do not change the date unless she can read the faint writing as well. If she cannot confirm the child, keep the current uncertainty rather than choosing the most likely face. The catalogue is meant to help the family compare evidence later, not to make the photographs seem more certain than they are.

Finally, keep the chest inventory with the catalogue and note that it includes the blue dish key, the grocery receipt, the postcard, the German note, and the negative sleeve. None of those loose items should be placed inside an envelope with a photograph until the family has reviewed the connections. The chest stays in the upstairs hall while the labels are checked, and the bottom drawer should be opened straight out rather than lifted at an angle because of the sticking runner. When Ruth visits next month, she can review the river names and the birthday group, but the catalogue should remain useful even if she cannot identify either one.

our shared bicycle shed sits behind the west entrance of Alder Court, between the laundry room and the low brick wall. It was put in place in 2019, and the residents' committee has kept a paper key register since then. The shed has twelve marked spaces, although there are usually more than twelve bicycles in it by Friday evening. The committee says the spaces are for residents, not visitors, but it has not made a separate rule about short visits. I use the shed most days, and I find the narrow entrance slightly awkward when I have panniers on both sides of my bike.

The roof is corrugated plastic, and its front edge is lower than the back edge, so rain runs toward the drain along the wall. One roof panel became loose during a windy night in March. Mara from apartment 2B tied it down temporarily with cord, and the committee arranged a repair the following week. The repaired panel is still a different shade from the others. On sunny afternoons the roof makes the shed bright enough to see the number tags, but the rear corner stays dim. There is one motion-sensor light there, and it comes on after a short delay. Residents have mentioned the delay a few times, though nobody has asked for the light to be replaced.

The entrance latch catches if the door is pulled shut too quickly. People sometimes leave it open while they move a bicycle through, which makes the latch issue less noticeable but leaves the doorway exposed to the rain. The committee posted a small sign saying, “Please pull the door until it clicks.” That has helped a little, especially when children are bringing in smaller bikes. The sign is attached with two screws, one of which is beginning to loosen. If the door does not latch after the next adjustment, the committee has said it will ask the caretaker to look at the frame as well. That condition matters because the caretaker is not being asked to work on the frame yet.

There are two floor pumps on the shelf beside the entrance. The blue pump belongs to the shed, and the silver one was left there by a resident who moved out last autumn. The blue pump has a pressure gauge that is hard to read, while the silver one has no gauge. I usually check tire pressure at home, so this is not a large problem for me, but other residents have borrowed the pumps before weekend rides. A handwritten note on the shelf says, “Put the pump back when you are finished.” It is clear enough, although the paper curls at the corners and is occasionally covered by gloves or a helmet.

1. Space and access: the painted numbers run from 1 to 12, with spaces 1 and 2 nearest the entrance. Space 12 is next to the rear wall, where a pipe narrows the available room. A long cargo bike can fit there only if its front wheel is turned toward the center aisle. The committee has not assigned spaces to particular apartments, and residents choose an open one when they arrive. There is no written limit on how long a bicycle may be left in the shed. At the last residents' meeting, someone asked whether an unused bike could be moved after a month, but the minutes record that the committee would discuss it later.

The floor is concrete, with a shallow channel leading to a drain near the back. Leaves and small bits of gravel collect in the channel after wet weather. Theo in 4A sweeps it out every couple of weeks, although he says he does it when he notices it rather than on a schedule. A small patch beside the drain is darker than the rest of the floor. It was already there when I moved into Alder Court, and I do not know what caused it. The caretaker looked at it last summer and said, “It seems dry at the moment.” No repair was arranged, and the patch has not visibly changed since then.

The committee keeps a box of spare reflectors, two cable ties, and a few paper labels in a cupboard inside the shed. The cupboard key is kept with the main shed key in the laundry-room office. To borrow something from the box, a resident is meant to write their apartment number in the register, but people do not always remember. Last month, someone left a note saying that a red rear reflector was missing. The committee added two reflectors to the box the next day, but it is not known whether either one was the original reflector. There are also three abandoned-looking locks on the shelf; nobody has identified their owners, so they have not been removed.

The lighting and access were discussed at the committee's February meeting. A resident in 6C said, “I can see the entrance, but not the back wheel when I am locking up.” Another resident said the sensor had worked fine for them. The minutes describe both comments, and say the committee will check the light when the electrician next visits the building. They do not give a date for that visit. The committee also agreed to replace the curling pump note with a plastic sleeve, but only if a spare sleeve can be found in the building office. If there is no spare sleeve, the note will stay as it is for now. I think the light is probably adequate for ordinary use, though the rear corner is harder to see on cloudy evenings.

Residents generally make room for one another, but the aisle can become crowded when several people arrive at the same time. Last Thursday, two bikes were being moved through the doorway while another resident was trying to turn a cargo bike near space 12. Everyone waited a moment, and the bikes went in without anyone needing to take one back outside. A small basket on the shelf holds discarded bell parts and reflectors, not items for general use. The committee has not decided what to do with the three locks or whether to introduce assigned spaces. For now, the numbered spaces remain open for residents to use, and the register and cupboard key are kept in the laundry-room office.

It identifies the person responsible for each shift, the expected checks, and the time at which any unfinished work must be handed over. The system is designed for a small team whose schedules overlap only briefly, so each entry needs to be clear enough for someone who did not see the previous shift.

Watering is planned around the condition of the plants rather than a fixed daily quantity. Staff check the surface and weight of representative pots, inspect the drainage trays, and compare their observations with the moisture notes recorded the day before. A dry-looking surface alone does not establish that a root ball needs water, particularly in the larger containers in Bay C. Conversely, seed trays in Bay A can dry quickly near the warm-air outlet, even when the surrounding benches feel cool. The person on duty records whether watering was needed, which bench was checked, and any unusual change in leaf color or growth. This gives the next shift a useful history without turning routine observations into diagnoses.

The regular rota runs from Monday through Saturday, with a shorter inspection on Sunday. The opening shift begins at 7:30 a.m. and checks the hose connections, water temperature, and the level in the rainwater tank before using the watering wand. The afternoon shift starts at 1:00 p.m. and reviews the morning notes before deciding whether a second check is necessary. Staff avoid watering leaves late in the day because damp foliage can remain wet overnight. When a scheduled check is postponed by deliveries or maintenance, the person responsible writes the revised time on the clipboard rather than leaving the next person to guess whether the task was completed.

1. **Bay A — propagation:** Check the moisture of the seed trays and plug cells at the front, center, and warm-air end of each bench. Use the narrow-spout can for small cells and apply water slowly, allowing it to soak in rather than run across the tray. If a tray is already evenly moist, record the check and do not water it again just to match another tray. Move any standing water from beneath the cells after the final check.
2. **Bay B — herbs and leafy crops:** Inspect one container from each bench and check the bed edges as well as the center. Water at soil level, taking care not to wash compost onto the walkway. The basil bench dries faster than the parsley bench on sunny days, but its condition still needs to be checked before watering. Mark any blocked drainage hole for the maintenance list.
3. **Bay C — fruiting plants:** Check the soil beside the stems without disturbing roots, and look for water in the saucers. Use the marked jug to keep the amount consistent when a pot requires water. Do not treat a curled leaf by itself as proof that a plant is dry; compare the soil and the latest temperature note first. Record any pot that remains unusually light after watering so it can be inspected again.
4. **Shared equipment:** Rinse the wand and cans after use, return them to their labeled hooks, and close the tank valve. If the hose coupling leaks, place the red tag on it and notify the shift lead before the next watering round. Do not leave a hose stretched across the central aisle, even when another person is expected to use it shortly afterward.

The rota includes a weather and temperature check because greenhouse conditions can change quickly when cloud cover shifts or a vent is left open. The thermometer beside Bay B is read at the start of both shifts, and the reading is written beside the date rather than in a separate notebook. If the overnight forecast is below 10°C, the closing shift checks that the vent levers are secured and tells the morning staff to assess the pots before opening the vents. This condition matters to the watering decision: cold, wet compost can remain saturated for longer, so the morning worker must rely on the pot checks and not assume that the usual early watering is appropriate. If the thermometer reading differs sharply from the forecast, the shift lead is informed and the discrepancy is recorded.

Several practical details help the rota work during busy periods. The rainwater tank usually supplies the greenhouse, while the mains tap is kept available if the tank level is too low for the planned round. Staff use the same clean, labeled hose for either source and note a change of supply on the clipboard. Fertilizer is not added as part of routine watering; any feeding is listed separately by the crop lead, with the date and mixture written down before it is prepared. A new worker should be shown how to read the jug marks and where to find the crop notes before being assigned a solo shift. The crop lead checks the clipboard each Wednesday and follows up on blank entries, repeated drainage problems, or observations that have not yet been addressed.

If a job cannot be completed before the shift ends, the outgoing worker writes the reason, the remaining task, and the time it was last checked.

The clipboard also holds a monthly rota sheet that names the primary and backup workers for each day. The backup is responsible only when the primary worker is absent or asks for help, and the change is noted so two people do not unknowingly repeat the same round. On public holidays, the shift lead confirms the reduced staffing plan at least two days beforehand and assigns the Sunday-style inspection if the usual afternoon shift is not covered. Delivery days are marked on the sheet because pallets sometimes block access to the tank or the main aisle. In that case, staff check which route remains safe before carrying water, and they record any bay they could not reach rather than moving heavy loads alone.

At the end of each week, the crop lead reviews the records for patterns that may help adjust the rota, such as one bench drying faster after a change in ventilation or repeated standing water beneath a particular group of pots. These observations guide future checks but do not automatically change the watering plan. A change to the assigned times, equipment, or crop responsibilities is written on the rota and dated so everyone can see when it took effect. The current sheet remains posted until its replacement is ready, and older sheets are filed in the greenhouse office for reference. Keeping those records together makes it possible to understand what was checked, what was left for the next shift, and how the greenhouse routine changed through the season.

Create a requirements brief for wakeclean, a small log-file cleanup utility for the fictional North Quay ferry operations team. This is a pilot, not a general-purpose product. Use the facts, proposals, and open questions below to describe expected behavior, reporting, and decisions that still need an owner. Do not write code or resolve policy questions that are not settled in the notes. Do not expand the work into a general log-management strategy.

## Environment and scope

The pilot would start on the two terminal hosts, quay-ops-01 and quay-ops-02. Both run Debian 12 Linux. A third Debian 12 host, quay-data-01, is in the office and is not part of the initial rollout. The log root on the terminal hosts is `/srv/harbor/logs`; the archive mount is `/mnt/archive/harbor`. The services in scope are ticket-api, berth-sync, and sensor-bridge. Wakeclean is intended to run unattended once configured. The team usually has one short maintenance window each month.

The current log directory is about 86 GB on each terminal host, whose disks are 120 GB total. Last week's rounded `du` figures were 54 GB for ticket-api, 19 GB for sensor-bridge, and about 13 GB for berth-sync plus rotated odds and ends. Treat these as estimates, not an exact inventory. Operators report that ticket-api grows fastest on busy sailing days and that sensor-bridge can produce a burst after a hardware reconnect.

Names mostly consist of a service name followed by a date; rotated files often end in `.gz`. Examples observed last week include `ticket-api-2025-03-18.log`, `ticket-api-2025-03-17.log.gz`, `berth-sync-2025-03-18.log`, and `sensor-bridge-2025-03-15.log.gz`. Unfamiliar items under the root include `deploy-notes.txt` and a folder named `handoff`. Their relationship to an application has not been confirmed. Describe the need for a defined handling policy for unrecognized names and identify it as an open decision. Do not assume that every old file under the root is disposable.

## Retention and archive policy

Routine application logs are intended to remain locally for 30 days. Incident logs are intended to remain for 180 days, but the team has not documented how an incident log is marked or who assigns that status. Audit logs must never be deleted automatically. The on-call lead currently copies incident material to the archive by hand and said, “the archive is a second copy, not permission to erase the audit trail.” Preserve the distinction between an archived copy and permission to delete.

It is unresolved whether wakeclean should move files, copy them, or only remove eligible local files after confirming an archived copy. Identify this as a decision for an owner; do not select an approach. The archive is not always reachable during the early shift. Ivo from systems said, “the archive is mounted, but it isn't always reachable during the early shift.” If `/mnt/archive/harbor` is unavailable at run start, the proposed policy is to delete no eligible files in that run and record the reason. Retain this condition.

## Operation and safety

The proposed schedule is 02:15 local time daily. Hosts use local time and may change clocks for daylight saving. Whether the schedule should follow wall-clock time or mean an elapsed 24 hours is unresolved; surface the question. Current free-space alerting begins at 75 percent disk use, but that alert is separate from cleanup policy. One operator wants the brief to clarify whether cleanup runs on schedule even when disk use is low or is triggered by the threshold. No choice has been made.

Mara, the terminal supervisor, said, “we're fine until Monday, and then ticket-api eats the free space.” Nia on call said that nobody wants a service restart as part of cleanup and that active log files must not be truncated while a service is writing to them. Treat these as constraints. If a safe method is needed to determine whether a file is active, leave the method for the requirements writer to specify. Hard links, symbolic links, and permissions on files owned by a service account have not been discussed. Identify them as policy questions rather than assuming behavior. Also cover what should happen if a file changes between inspection and action.

A dry-run mode is required and should be the default for the first pilot configuration. It should show which files would be acted on and why, without changing them. Distinguish dry-run output from an actual run. The candidate policy from the operations meeting is to require a separate operator acknowledgement before deletion when more than 2 GB of files would be removed in one run. The team has not decided what counts as acknowledgement for an unattended daily job. Preserve the threshold and identify the acknowledgement method as an open question; do not invent a mechanism.

## Reporting requirements

Write each run's report under `/var/log/wakeclean/reports` on the host. The requested CSV header is:

`run_time,host,path,action,reason,size_bytes,result`

Include one row per considered file, including skipped files. The example given was `ticket-api-2025-03-17.log.gz` marked as skipped because it is inside the 30-day window. This is an example, not a decision about the exact boundary of the age policy. Include a final run summary with counts and bytes considered, removed, and skipped. Reports should distinguish dry runs from real runs and record errors when a file could not be examined. It is unresolved whether the summary belongs in the same CSV or a separate file. Reports may expose paths and filenames, so identify report access and retention as questions rather than prescribing values.

## Topics to cover

1. Scope and host rollout.
2. Eligible and protected files, retention rules, and the unresolved incident marker.
3. Archive checks and deletion behavior.
4. Scheduling and the disk-space trigger.
5. Dry-run behavior and operator acknowledgement.
6. Active files, links, permissions, and files that change between inspection and action.
7. Report fields, run summaries, and error handling.
8. Open decisions and an owner to identify for each.

Keep the brief usable by the operations and systems teams without presenting unsettled policy as complete. The practical risk should remain clear in the closing portion: disk pressure is already being noticed, while retention, archive, and unattended-approval rules are not all resolved. Ask the brief writer to state what must be decided before unattended deletion begins; do not declare the pilot approved or ready.

we started the meal calendar because the old arrangement was getting hard to follow, especially when people changed plans by text and then forgot to tell everyone else. the calendar is on the kitchen wall beside the grocery list, and there is also a shared copy on the family tablet. Mara updates the paper one on Sunday evenings, usually after she has checked which nights she will be home late. The tablet copy is useful when someone is away, though we have not made it the only version because Grandpa prefers to look at the wall. I think the two copies are mostly easy to keep in line, but occasionally one gets updated before the other.

The calendar covers Monday through Sunday and has a space for the main meal, the person cooking, and anything that needs to come out of the freezer. We do not put breakfast or lunch on it, since those meals are less predictable. The squares are a little narrow for long notes, so we use a separate sticky note for details such as a recipe name or a reminder to buy more rice. On the first Sunday of each month, Mara draws a fresh grid rather than trying to erase the old one. That makes the writing clearer, although it means the markers need to stay near the calendar instead of in the desk drawer.

1. Monday and Tuesday are generally the simplest nights to plan. Mara works from home on Monday and can start dinner earlier, while Leo has a class on Tuesday and usually gets back after seven. If Leo's class is canceled, he can cook Tuesday instead, but he needs to text Mara before noon so she can change the name on the calendar. Otherwise, the meal stays as written, even if he gets home sooner than expected. We have had a few crossed messages about that, because a text in the family chat is not always seen by everyone.
2. Wednesday is set aside for leftovers when there are enough portions. If there is not enough food from earlier in the week, Nina makes soup or a simple pasta dish. She would perhaps rather have a clear rule about what counts as enough, but the portions vary and nobody wants to measure them. The calendar therefore says “leftovers, if there are enough,” rather than promising that we will use them. This wording is slightly fussy, but it has stopped people from assuming a particular dish will be available.
3. Thursday is Grandpa's choice, unless he has an appointment that evening. When he is out, we move his choice to Friday if the Friday plan is flexible; otherwise, we leave Thursday blank and decide later. He often asks for baked potatoes, but he has also suggested lentil stew and omelets. The calendar lists his choice only after he has said what he wants, rather than putting baked potatoes there every week. That keeps the plan accurate without making his preferences seem fixed.

Friday is usually the night we make something that takes longer, because most people are home and there is less pressure to eat at a particular time. We have used the slot for vegetable lasagna, roast chicken, and homemade pizza, but none of those meals is required. Mara sometimes writes “something from the oven” when she has not settled on a recipe. That is enough information for grocery planning, as long as the ingredients are added to the list before the store trip. If we are going to use a recipe that needs a special ingredient, whoever chose it has to write that ingredient on the list; the rest of the family should not have to guess.

Saturday is open for visits or plans outside the house. We leave the meal square empty until we know whether anyone is coming over, and we do not count an empty square as a missed assignment. If guests are expected, the person who invited them puts the number of guests on the calendar, even if the menu is still undecided. This matters because the dining table seats six comfortably, and a larger group may mean borrowing folding chairs from the basement. I do not think we need to plan every guest meal in advance, but it helps to know how many people are coming before Saturday afternoon.

Sunday is our shared cooking day, though not everyone has to be in the kitchen at once. We usually make one meal together and prepare one extra item for the week, such as washed vegetables or a pot of beans. Nina prefers to choose the main dish by Friday so she can check what is already in the pantry. Leo is happy to help chop, but he does not want to be assigned the same job every week. The calendar has a small initials space for anyone who has volunteered, rather than a fixed rotation. If nobody has volunteered by Saturday night, Mara asks in the family chat before she adds names herself.

The notes at the bottom of the calendar are for information that applies to more than one day. Right now they say that there is a bag of frozen peas in the freezer, Grandpa does not like raw onion, and the large soup pot is on the lower pantry shelf. We remove a note when it is no longer useful, but we do not write down every ingredient we have. The freezer reminder is updated after someone uses the peas, and the onion note stays because it affects several recipes. These small details have made the calendar more practical than a list of meals alone.

We are still figuring out whether the tablet copy is worth the extra effort. Mara enters the week there after updating the wall calendar, and the rest of us can view it, but not everyone remembers to check it. Perhaps we will try sending one Sunday reminder in the family chat, although I would rather not have the calendar turn into another stream of messages. For now, the wall version remains the one we rely on at home, and the tablet is a backup for people who are out. At the end of each week, Mara looks over both copies and fixes any difference before drawing the next grid.

The order form at Juniper Street Bakery is getting a revision for the spring season, and I have been looking at how customers use it. The shop is on the corner of Juniper and Ninth, with a counter for walk-in purchases and a separate table where preorders are collected. The printed form and the website ask for the same information, but the questions are not in the same order. That is making a few customers call the shop to check whether they have missed a step. Mara, who manages the bakery, says the form should feel straightforward even to someone placing an order for the first time. I usually think the printed version is easier to follow, though perhaps that is because I see it at the counter each week.

The first section asks for a customer’s name, phone number, and email address, followed by the date the order is needed. At present, the date field is small, and people sometimes write the pickup time where the date should go. The bakery is open Tuesday through Sunday, from 7 a.m. until 4 p.m., and it does not take Monday pickups. Mara asked for the available pickup days to be listed beside the date field instead of being explained in a note at the bottom. The form also asks whether the customer wants to be contacted by phone or email if staff need to clarify a detail. “We don’t want to guess about a cake message,” Mara said. That choice should remain optional, since most orders do not need a follow-up.

Pickup timing matters because the small front refrigerator has limited room, and decorated cakes are kept in the back until they are due to be collected. The customer can choose a time in half-hour increments, from 9 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. The bakery cannot promise a pickup outside those hours. If an order is for a same-day pickup, the customer must call before placing it online; the website form is intended for orders placed at least one day ahead. That condition is easy to miss in the current version, where it appears after the payment details. Mara would like it next to the pickup date, where it can be seen before a customer chooses a time.

The product section needs to show the choices more clearly, without suggesting that every item can be customized in every way. The regular menu includes round cakes in six-inch and nine-inch sizes, a rectangular sheet cake, cupcakes by the dozen, and two kinds of cookie boxes. The cake flavors are vanilla, chocolate, lemon, and carrot. Buttercream is available in vanilla or chocolate, while the carrot cake comes with cream cheese frosting only. The form currently puts frosting choices beneath all the flavors, which has led to requests for chocolate frosting on carrot cake. Mara said, “We can make the options clear without making the page feel like a rulebook.” The form should say that frosting selection applies to vanilla, chocolate, and lemon cakes, and that carrot cake has cream cheese frosting.

1. For a round cake, the customer should mark one size and one flavor. The six-inch cake serves about eight people, and the nine-inch one serves about eighteen. Those serving counts are estimates, not guarantees, because slices vary in size. The sheet cake is listed as serving about twenty-four, and cupcakes are sold by the dozen, with a minimum order of one dozen. Cookie boxes come in a dozen or two dozen, and the choices are oatmeal raisin or chocolate chip. The customer can request a mix of cookie types in the notes, but the bakery may need to call if the requested split is unclear. These quantities should be shown next to each item rather than collected in a general notes field.

The allergy question is currently a blank line labeled “special requests,” which is too broad to help staff sort the information. The revised form should ask whether the order needs an allergy note and provide room to name the ingredient. Juniper Street Bakery uses wheat, eggs, milk, peanuts, and tree nuts in its kitchen, and it cannot promise that an item is free of traces from shared equipment. Mara wants the form to state that limitation plainly, while still allowing customers to tell the bakery about an allergy. “Please don’t make it sound like we can guarantee a safe product,” she said. This note belongs beside the allergy field, not in tiny print at the end. Customers can also use the same space for a non-allergy dietary question, but the bakery will contact them before confirming whether it can meet that request.

For celebration cakes, the form has a separate message box with room for up to thirty characters, including spaces. The staff can write a short message in icing, but they do not offer custom drawings through the order form. Customers can choose a border color from white, pink, blue, or green, and can ask for no border. The color is a request rather than a promise, because the shade may look slightly different on different frosting. If someone needs a particular color for an event, Mara prefers that they call the bakery to discuss it before submitting the order. The form should keep the message and border choices together, but it should not imply that the message can be longer than the character limit or that a drawing is available.

Payment is due when the customer places the order, either at the counter or through the website. The shop accepts cash and card at the counter, and the website accepts card only. The current printed form asks for payment details before customers have selected their products, which can feel out of order. Mara would rather move payment to the last section. Orders can be changed up to 48 hours before pickup by calling the shop; after that point, staff may not be able to change the product or message. If a customer cancels at least 48 hours before pickup, the payment is refunded. The form should distinguish that cancellation condition from a late change, since the two requests do not have the same result.

Once a form is received, the counter staff copy the order date and pickup time onto the daily sheet, while the baker checks the flavors, quantities, and any allergy note. The daily sheet has space for twelve orders, so a busy Saturday may take more than one page. The bakery uses paper forms at the counter because some customers prefer not to order online, and those forms are kept in a drawer beside the receipt printer until they are entered on the sheet. The website sends a confirmation email after submission, but the printed form does not create an automatic confirmation. Staff tell counter customers their order details aloud before taking payment, which gives them a chance to catch a mistaken date or phone number.

The packaging question should remain near the end of the form. Customers can request a cake box with a window, a plain cake box, or separate cupcake carriers, depending on what they order. The bakery does not currently offer reusable containers, and customers cannot bring their own packaging for an order placed through the website. At the counter, a customer can ask about bringing a clean container before placing the order, but staff need to check whether it fits the item. Mara says the packaging choices are useful, but she would keep the wording brief so customers do not mistake them for different product sizes. The form should also leave enough space for a note about carrying the order by hand or taking it on a bus, since those details occasionally affect which package is practical.

This is my account of the equipment return at Cedar Ridge School on the last afternoon before the winter break. The return covered the science rooms, the art studio, and the small media lab, and it was handled in the north receiving room because the main office was still being used for family conferences. I arrived just after one with the printed inventory and a blue crate of spare tags. The room had three folding tables and a clear lane to the loading door, so students could bring in carts without crossing the line for the office. The principal had asked us to finish the count before the custodian locked the outside gate at four, but nobody was expected to rush through checks just to meet that time.

Mara Ellis was the science department aide, and she brought the two science carts over from room twenty-four. Mr. Cho brought the media equipment himself, and Elena Ruiz from the art studio came with a student helper named Cal. We checked the names against the return sheet rather than assuming that whoever carried an item owned it. The carts had been used by different classes, and their labels were not always current. Mara said, “The seventh grade borrowed the small microscope case on Tuesday, but it came back to room twenty-four before lunch.” The sign-out card showed the same thing, and the case was on her cart. The media room still had one camera checked out to the yearbook group, so Mr. Cho had written that down instead of marking it returned.

At the first table, we sorted the science equipment by room and type. The two carts had six microscopes, eight trays of prepared slides, four power leads, and a sealed box of replacement bulbs. The fourth microscope had a loose eyepiece, but it still focused, and the problem was already written on its service card. We did not call it new damage because the card was dated October and the teacher had initialed it. The slide trays were dry, and each lid was shut except the tray marked pond life, which had one corner clip missing. I put a yellow tag on that tray and wrote “missing clip” in the condition column. The spare clips were in a drawer in the prep room, but that room had been locked after the chemistry class left, so we left the tray as it was rather than borrowing an uncounted part.

We had a brief question about the handheld meters because the label on the return sheet said four and the shelf card said five. There were four meters in the blue bin, and the fifth was still signed out to Mr. Cho for the energy lesson on Monday. The correction mattered because the return sheet had to show what was physically present and what was still assigned to a teacher. I crossed out the earlier count with one line and entered four in the box beside “returned.” I left the fifth meter on the outstanding list with Mr. Cho’s name. The Monday lesson was not canceled, and nobody asked us to mark the equipment as returned early.

1. Check the item and its label.
2. Compare the number with the return sheet.
3. Look over the condition and record existing damage.
4. Place anything needing attention in the yellow tag area.
5. Get the person returning it to initial the line.

We used that order for the remaining items, and Cal read the item names while Elena checked the art list. There were twelve drawing boards, ten metal rulers, and three portable lamps. The boards had small paint marks on the reverse side, and those marks were not listed as damage because the boards were already designated for paint work. One lamp had a frayed cord near the plug, so Elena kept it on the table and wrote that it should not be plugged in. The other two lamps had intact cords. The rulers were all present, though one was bent slightly near the end, and that bend was described on the previous sheet.

Mr. Cho’s camera was still with the yearbook group, and he showed us a message from their adviser saying the last interview was being recorded in the library until three. The return rule allowed equipment to stay out if the borrower and an expected return time were written on the sheet, so we entered the adviser as the responsible borrower and three o’clock as the expected time. This was a condition for leaving the camera off the receiving table, not a statement that it had already come back. The camera case and charger were at school, and Mr. Cho set both beside the media shelf while we waited. He said, “I can bring the camera down when the students finish, but I cannot promise they will be done before the bell.” We left the camera line open and did not put a return initial beside it.

At about two forty, the yearbook students came into the room with the camera, and the memory card was inside its labeled case. We checked the camera number and the charger number separately because the charger had a different asset label. The camera body was clean, and the strap buckle was intact. The battery showed one bar, but there was no requirement to charge it before return, so we wrote the battery level in the notes and plugged the charger into the return bin. The adviser confirmed that the final interview had been saved and then initialed the line herself because she was listed as borrower. The student who carried the case did not sign for her.

Before the gate was locked, I compared the pages again. The science carts were assigned to room twenty-four; the four meters were marked returned, and one meter remained on the outstanding list for Monday. The tagged microscope tray and the lamp with the frayed cord were held apart from equipment ready for storage. The three lamps were still recorded as present because two were safe to store and one was not ready for use. The camera and charger were both present, and the camera return time was written beside the adviser’s initials. Cal took the art boards and rulers back to the studio while Elena carried the lamps to the locked workbench where the cord could be examined. The receiving room table was cleared except for the yellow tag tray and the folder of signed sheets. When I left, the gate was still open, and the folder was with Mara in the receiving room.

The shelf is for neighbors to borrow games for up to three weeks, with no fee, and people can ask for an extension if nobody else is waiting. We have about sixty games, but the list taped to the cabinet is from January and a few things have changed since then. I want the guide to be practical for whoever is on duty, not a big policy document.

The center is open Tuesday and Thursday from 4 to 7, and Saturday from 10 to 1. There is usually one volunteer at the front desk, but on Saturday a second person sometimes comes in to help with the shelf. People bring games back to the desk, not directly to the shelves, because some boxes have been left in the wrong place. If a game is returned while a volunteer is on duty, the volunteer should check the box against the inventory card. If every listed piece is there and the box is not visibly damaged, mark it returned and put it back in its labeled section. If pieces are missing or the box is damaged, mark it as on hold and keep it in the gray cabinet until someone checks it; please make those two paths easy to see in the guide. We don't want a held game going back out just because someone has put it on the shelf.

There also needs to be a clear alternative for returns outside those hours. If nobody is at the desk when a person arrives, they can put the game in the blue return crate under the sign-in table, but they should not put it on the shelf or in the gray cabinet. The next volunteer checks the crate at the start of their shift and follows the same inventory check before deciding where it goes. The crate is only for returned games, not donations, forms, or games people are asking about. Last month, a donation ended up mixed in with returns, and we couldn't tell who had left it, so the sign should say where donations go instead: to the front desk volunteer for now.

1. Borrowing and due dates: Please explain that a borrower writes their name, a phone number or email, the game title, and the date borrowed on the paper log. They choose either contact detail, not both. A game is due three weeks from the date it was borrowed, and the volunteer writes the due date in the log as well. The borrower can ask for one extension of up to two weeks. If no one else is waiting for that title, the volunteer may extend it and write the new due date; if someone is waiting, the due date stays as it is and the volunteer tells the borrower there is a request for it. Please don't make it sound as though extensions happen automatically.

2. Waiting requests: The request sheet is kept in the clear folder at the desk. A person can ask for a particular title in person or by calling the center, and a volunteer writes down their name, one contact detail, the title, and the date they asked. When a copy is ready, the volunteer contacts the first person on the sheet and holds it for three open days. If that person doesn't pick it up in that time, move to the next name rather than keeping it aside indefinitely. If a held game is waiting for a missing piece to be checked, leave the request date in place; don't treat it as ready or contact the next person until the game has been checked and marked available. That part matters because people have asked why their place changed while a box was being looked at.

3. What to do if something is wrong: Volunteers can use the short condition note inside each box. It lists the title, the usual number of pieces, and any special setup parts that are easy to overlook. If a piece is missing, write the piece and game title on the yellow repair slip and leave it with the box in the gray cabinet. If the box is wet, torn, or otherwise hard to close, write that on the same slip too. Please don't throw out a damaged box or substitute a piece from another game. The shelf coordinator, Mina Patel, checks the cabinet on Thursday evenings, but volunteers should still make the hold mark when they receive the game, rather than waiting for Mina to come by.

People have been asking what happens when they return a game after the center has closed, so include the crate steps near the opening, not buried at the end. A paper log entry stays open until the return has been checked, even if the borrower says all the pieces are there. The guide should say that in a simple way. A volunteer can tell the borrower, “Thanks, I’ll check it before I put it back,” but should not promise that the game is available right away. If a return is in the blue crate and the box has no inventory card, set it aside for Mina instead of guessing from the title on the lid. We sometimes have different editions of the same game, and their parts are not always interchangeable.

4. Shelf layout and questions: The sections are family games, strategy games, party games, and children’s games. The labels are on the front edges of the shelves, and the alphabetical list is in the clear folder beside the log. If a volunteer cannot tell which section fits a title, they can leave it at the desk for the next shift rather than choosing at random. The guide should mention that visitors are welcome to ask for help finding a game, but volunteers should not promise that a title is on the shelf before checking the log and the hold area. The log is a record of borrowing, not a live count, so there can be a short delay after a return.

Please keep the friendly voice that the center uses. One parent told us, “It’s helpful when someone explains the pieces before we take it home,” so it may be useful to say that a volunteer can answer basic questions about a game if they know it. They don't need to teach the whole game, and they can say they are unsure when they haven't played it. There is also a small printed card inside the front cover with the designer and player count for some games, but not all of them. Don't imply that every box has that card. We don't collect a deposit, and we don't ask people to show identification; the log's contact detail is what we use if we need to follow up about a late return.

The new guide will be printed on two sheets and kept in a plastic sleeve beside the sign-in table, with one copy in the gray cabinet for volunteers. Please organize these details so the opening gives the return choices, followed by the borrowing and waiting-request steps, then the damaged-game process and shelf questions. Keep the numbered sections, but make the instructions readable when someone is standing at the desk with a line of visitors. If a detail is unclear in these notes, leave it as written rather than filling in a new center rule. The important thing is that volunteers can tell what to do with a checked return, a return left after hours, and a game that is still on hold.
